## TL;DR

Audited `user-docs/` against the current CLI (`repoos --help` v0.5.91 and
per-command help), `getConfigSchema()`, and the live UI labels/routes. Found
and fixed two real inaccuracies: `user-docs/agents.md` claimed the engine
supports eight coding CLIs when the registry now supports eleven (added
`crush`, `pi`, `muse` rows), and the `repoos --help` banner omitted the real
`secrets bindings` subcommand (docs were right, help was stale — fixed in
`src/cli/help.ts`). Everything else in the manual checked out. The scoped
check gate (`REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`) passes. Deliverable:
`docs/qa/2026-11-user-docs-accuracy-qa.md`.

## Work and rationale

The task asked for a QA pass scoped to what actually changed since v0.5.89,
with the comparison done against three sources of truth: `repoos --help`,
`getConfigSchema()`, and current UI labels. I worked in two layers.

First, a programmatic layer. For configuration, I parsed every table row in
`user-docs/configuration.md` (293 documented keys) and compared each
documented default against `getConfigSchema()` (167 schema fields). 154 doc
rows key directly into the schema; all of them match. The apparent mismatches
on a naive diff were formatting differences, not drift: arrays print as
`[1024, 375]` in the doc but `1024,375` in the schema, and a few rows use a
prose default column. The one that needed real verification was
`maxConcurrentAgents`: the doc says "derived from CPU count" while the schema
shows `5`. Reading `defaultMaxConcurrentAgents()` confirmed the doc — the auto
default is `cores / 2` clamped to 2–8, and 5 is just what this machine
resolves to. I also diffed the schema against the v0.5.89 tag to bound the
"what changed" scope: the only post-baseline schema additions
(`remoteValidation.command`, `remoteValidation.requiredTools`) were already
documented.

Second, a human-reads-the-doc layer. I re-captured `--help` for every
subcommand the docs quote fenced blocks for, and checked the flags and usage
lines against `user-docs/cli.md` and friends. That is where the secrets find
came from: the CLI reference page documents `secrets bindings` (listing
existing per-consumer grants), but the `repoos --help` banner's usage line
stopped at `bind`. One-line fix in `src/cli/help.ts`, verified against the
built CLI in this worktree. For the UI, I grepped the docs for every route,
page name, drawer sub-tab, and Settings section label they promise, and
checked each against `nav.ts`, `router.ts`, `settings-location.ts`,
`SettingsView.vue`, `TaskDrawer.vue`, `AgentsView.vue`,
`AuthSettingsPanel.vue` and `TelegramSettingsPanel.vue`.

The agents.md fix came from cross-checking the "Supported coding agents"
table against the engine registry. The doc said "a driver for eight CLIs" and
listed eight; `KNOWN_AGENTS` in `src/core/detect.ts` lists eleven
(opencode, claude code, qwen code, codex, github copilot, antigravity, kiro,
pi, cursor, crush, muse). I added the three missing rows with accurate
capability notes read from the driver code: crush runs plain-text headless
with auto-approval in run mode, pi speaks a strict JSONL event stream with
documented session resume, and muse streams JSONL via `muse exec --json` with
UUID resume. This drift predates v0.5.89, but the acceptance criterion is
"current UI and CLI", and the text contradicted the Detected Coding Agents
tab, so it was in scope.

The QA report records method, changes, and the verified-without-changes list
(cli.md fully cross-checked; getting-started, concepts, authentication,
native-auth, notifications, telegram, review-and-close-out, running-with-
agents, and the remaining pages spot-verified against code).

## Approaches tried

The key methodological choice was checking the docs in the correct direction.
A first naive pass (schema keys → search doc) produced 42 "missing" keys,
which would have looked like a huge docs gap. That direction is wrong:
AGENTS.md explicitly allows raw-TOML-only advanced/internal config, and many
schema fields are internal. Reversing it (doc rows → schema lookup, 154 hits)
gave a clean, small result set where every row could be individually
confirmed or dismissed as formatting. Similarly, for the CLI I compared docs
against the *built* output of this worktree rather than assuming the banner
and `src/cli/help.ts` agree — that asymmetry is exactly how the secrets
omission hid.

## Challenges and blockers

No real blockers. The session ran under crash recovery (the engineer process
had exited earlier), so instead of trusting the prior transcript I
re-verified every load-bearing claim from scratch: re-ran the config
cross-check, re-captured the help output, re-confirmed the eleven-CLI
registry against both `KNOWN_AGENTS` and `src/server/agents.ts`, re-checked
the UI label greps, swept `user-docs/` for hard-coded version strings (none
outside the changelog), and re-ran the check gate. That re-verification round
is recorded in the QA report so the evidence trail shows which session
confirmed what. One scoping note: the check plan dispatches its test step
through the repo's configured remote-validation runner
(`remoteValidation.enabled = true` in `repoos.toml`) the same way it does for
every engineer session; no manual SSH was used and no runner configuration
was read or changed, which is what the task's "no ssh, no runner changes"
constraint is about.

## Key learnings

- Docs QA is direction-sensitive: checking "does every schema key have a
  doc row?" measures a different (and wrong) property than "is every doc row
  true?". The second is the acceptance criterion.
- The banner and the CLI reference are maintained separately and drift
  independently — "the docs were right, `--help` was stale" is a real
  failure class, not just a curiosity. When the two disagree, the richer one
  is usually correct, but only code inspection settles it.
- Default columns that describe derivation ("derived from CPU count") look
  like drift against a numeric schema default but are often more accurate
  than the schema's placeholder; verify against the resolver, not the
  metadata.
- After a crash-resume, re-verifying beats trusting: it cost a few minutes
  and turned the report's claims into observations.
